new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for caro1242, so nothing to agree with or contradict. This is the first placement statement found, but it is a Proto-Trukic reconstruction applied to the daughter languages (including CRL) rather than a synchronic description of Saipan Carolinian; the Carolinian-specific text only attests that word-internal vowels differ in stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Proto-Trukic (a reconstruction, not a statement about the modern language): stress falls on the penultimate mora and on every second mora to its left, i.e. a mora-counting, right-to-left alternating pattern. For modern Saipan Carolinian the dissertation states only that adjacent vowels differ in degree of stress (the bw fricative allophone appears after the more strongly stressed vowel); it gives no placement rule. The 'basic phonetic information' section for Saipan Carolinian (pp. 159-163) covers consonants, vowels, gemination and vowel sequences, not stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Proto-Trukic reconstruction only: stress on every second mora to the left of the penultimate mora (alternating). Nothing on secondary stress in the modern language. Also p. 67: Goodenough's (1963) reconstructed *canucanu 'wet, watery' "with stress on the first and third syllables", cited in the history of Trukic reduplication.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The author calls the stress-conditioned reflex percentages 'not as clean as one might like' (p. 223).
new_statements.identity_note: Jackson 1983 splits Saipan Carolinian into a southern dialect CRL (descendants of Satawal, Lamotrek, Elato and Pullap migrants) and a northern dialect CRN (Namonuito/Ulul migrants); the p. 160 stress remark is for CRL, and the p. 223 rule is for Proto-Trukic as a whole. Fritz 1911 describes the 'Central Carolinian' speech of the atolls west of Truk as spoken by the Saipan Carolinians in the German period, i.e. the ancestor of today's southern (CRL) dialect.
